title: Seat a jig plate on its round and diamond locating pins, the one way round it fits
instruction: Put the jig plate on the fixture over both locating pins.
context: Before machining, a jig plate is lowered onto the fixture's locating pins so every part is worked in the same place. The pins differ in size, so the plate fits only one way round. Done by: machinists and machine setters (O*NET 51-4041, 51-4081). Unlike TK-7JBY7Y (a cover over one hidden dowel), TK-TPC59R (pick the pin that fits a hole), TK-BCUA5Y (two identical keyhole studs) and TK-NPBJ69 (a chip turned to a printed key), the new part is matching which hole goes on which pin.
setup: Positions are from the robot's view: 'in front' is distance away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are the robot's, the midline is halfway between the two arm bases, heights are above the table top. Fixture (dark-grey steel, 5 kg, clamped in reality): a base bar 4 cm front to back, 20 cm wide and 2 cm tall, running side to side, with two blue steel locating pins 12 mm tall with flat, unchamfered tops standing on its front-to-back centre line, 90 mm apart, their midpoint 3 cm off the bar's centre: a round pin 20 mm across, and a diamond pin 10 mm across the pins' line and 8 mm along it. Lot A (the screenshot): the bar centred 32 cm in front on the midline, the round pin 1.5 cm left and the diamond pin 7.5 cm right of the midline. Riser (fixed, grey steel): a bar 4 cm front to back, 12 cm side to side and 2 cm tall, centred 42 cm in front and 17 cm right of the midline. Jig plate (loose, gold anodised aluminium, 0.2 kg): 14 x 7 cm, 8 mm thick, with two square through-holes on its long centre line, 90 mm apart: a 26 mm hole 3.5 cm from the plate's middle and a 16 mm hole 5.5 cm from it on the other side. In lot A it lies flat on the riser, centred, its long sides turned 15 degrees anticlockwise (seen from above) from side to side, the 16 mm hole at the left-hand end. Lot B: the fixture turned end for end (round pin 1.5 cm right, diamond pin 7.5 cm left of the midline) with its centre 32.8 cm in front; the plate as in lot A. Lot C: the fixture as in lot A but centred 31.3 cm in front and 1.2 cm left of the midline; the plate turned end for end on the riser about its middle (the 16 mm hole at the right-hand end, long sides still 15 degrees anticlockwise from side to side). Lot D: the fixture turned end for end, centred 32.5 cm in front and 1 cm right of the midline (round pin 2.5 cm right, diamond pin 6.5 cm left); the plate as in lot C. Nothing else is on the table. Trials are run on lots A, B, C and D and averaged; the screenshot shows lot A.
scoring: Pass/fail, judged on a final photo, a ruler and the video. Score 1.0 if the plate has been let go (no part of either gripper within 5 mm of it) and lies still and flat on the fixture's bar (every corner of its underside within 1.5 mm of the bar's top), with the round pin through the 26 mm hole (its centre at most 3 mm off the hole's centre each way) and the diamond pin wholly inside the 16 mm hole (either face of the plate up), and the fixture was never moved more than 5 mm or turned more than 3 degrees from where its lot puts it at any time in the trial. Score 0 for anything else: the plate turned end for end (it then rests on the round pin's top), resting on a pin top, tilted, beside the pins, back on the riser, on the table, still moving, or held; or the fixture shoved, even if put back. The trial ends at 1.0 once that state has held for 3 s; otherwise it scores the last step. Trials are run on each of lots A, B, C and D and averaged.
reset_notes: Lift the plate off the pins and lay it back on the riser for the next lot (A and B: 16 mm hole at the left-hand end; C and D: turned end for end), long sides 15 degrees anticlockwise from side to side. Set the fixture for the lot (A: centred 32 cm out on the midline, round pin on the left; B: turned end for end, 32.8 cm out; C: round pin on the left, 31.3 cm out and 1.2 cm left; D: turned end for end, 32.5 cm out and 1 cm right) and clamp it. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Different-sized locating pins are a standard mistake-proofing practice: a part keyed this way fits only one way round. Here a 20 mm round pin and a 10 x 8 mm diamond pin fit only the 26 mm and 16 mm holes. Rigid boxes and cylinders, friction 1.2; holes are square. Each hole gives about 3 mm of play, so this tests orientation and placement, not fine registration. The fixture is a heavy loose part so lots can move it. Lots stop fixed habits, not a memorised replay of all four layouts.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (0 in each of lots A, B, C and D); demo: 1.0 in each lot
